Then compare your notes with your own last match and pick one thing to train that week.

Key takeaways

  • Watch one player in your position, not the ball. Most of their game happens off the ball.
  • Go in with one question and track two to five things with tally marks.
  • Split what you see by phase: your team has the ball, the opponent has it, and the seconds after it changes hands.
  • Compare with your own match (film it if you can) and pick one countable target for the week.
  • One focused half every week beats three full matches watched as a fan.

Practical tip: use full-match replays or extended highlights if you can, because normal highlights only show the ball. If you only have a TV broadcast, accept that your player will sometimes be off-screen and note what you can.

3. Set up so you can actually take notes

  • Turn the commentary off. Pundits talk about the ball and the score. You want your own read of one player.
  • Watch one half, not the full 90. 45 focused minutes is plenty at the start. Pause and rewind when something happens off-screen.
  • Use short codes so you don't miss the next action while writing. Make your own or use these:
CodeMeaning
S / S2Scanned once / scanned both shoulders before receiving
O / CBody open / closed when receiving
T+ / T= / T-First touch forward / sideways / backwards
R-in / R-to / R-dragRun in behind / towards the ball / run that drags a defender away
L-P / L-C / L-XAfter losing the ball: pressed / covered space / switched off

What to watch in each phase of play

A football match has four phases: your team has the ball, the opponent has the ball, and the two moments when the ball changes hands. Analysts and coaches split games this way, and it works for players too, because your job changes in each phase. Note which phase each of your tallies comes from.

PhaseWhat it meansWhat to watch your player do
In possessionTheir team has the ballWhere they stand to offer a pass, scans before receiving, body shape, first touch, the runs they make
Out of possessionThe opponent has the ballTheir position in the team's shape, who they mark, when they step out to press and when they hold
Defensive transitionTheir team has just lost the ballThe first 3 seconds: press the ball, cover a space, or switch off
Attacking transitionTheir team has just won the ballDo they run forward straight away, offer a safe pass, or stay in position?

Set pieces (corners, free kicks, throw-ins) can be a fifth row if your question is about them. Keep it simple at first: most players learn the most from the in-possession and transition rows, because that's where scanning, movement and reactions show.

Why so much off the ball? The FA's performance analysis team says a typical top-level game has about 58 minutes of in-play time. Your player has the ball for only a small part of that, so what they do in the rest of it is most of their game.

How to film and review your own match

The easiest way to analyse your own performance is to film your match from high up and watch it back with the same five rows you use for pros. You don't need a pro camera. A phone on a tripod, filmed from the stand or a raised spot near the halfway line, shows enough to count scans, body shape and runs.

  • Ask first. Check with your coach or club before filming, and follow their rules about filming other players.
  • Film wide, not zoomed. You need to see yourself and the space around you, not just the ball.
  • Get someone to film. A parent, friend or injured teammate can follow the play so you stay in the shot.
  • Watch it twice. First time, just watch. Second time, follow only yourself and fill in the worksheet.
  • Be fair to yourself. Write down what you did well too. The goal is one clear gap, not a list of everything wrong.

No video? Write your notes within 24 hours while you still remember, and ask one teammate one specific question, like "Did I check my shoulder before receiving in midfield?"

Does watching football make you a better player?

Watching as a fan helps a little. Watching with a plan helps more: one player, one question, notes, then testing what you learned in your own training and matches.

How long should it take to analyse a football match?

Start with one half, about 45 minutes of watching plus 10 minutes to fill in your notes. Pausing and rewinding adds time but is worth it. Once a week is enough if you then train what you found.

Can you analyse a football match from highlights?

Only a little. Highlights follow the ball, so they show shots and goals but hide most of what your player does off the ball. Use full-match replays or extended highlights whenever you can.

What is the difference between match analysis and player analysis?

Match analysis looks at how both teams played in one game: shape, pressing and patterns. Player analysis follows one person's job across the game. As a player trying to improve, player analysis of someone in your position is more useful.

Should I watch with the commentary on?

Turn it off when you are analysing. Commentators mostly talk about the ball, the score and big moments, which pulls your attention away from the one player you are studying and the question you set.
